One promising strategy for promoting high-quality cancer information consumption is through targeted interventions that are intentionally designed to reach individuals in the web-based spaces they occupy. However, there is a paucity of evidence-based information on the best strategies for designing and implementing web-based health behavior change interventions to improve individuals’cancer-related knowledge and prevent cancer. Objective: This study aimed to develop and pilot test a theory-based intervention via the web to reduce 6 cancer risk factors among rural emerging adults (EAs) through community-engaged research. Methods: This mixed methods evaluation describes the development of a web-based cancer prevention intervention aimed at rural EAs aged 18-26 years in the United States and delivered in Facebook private groups. The intervention was guided by behavior change theory and cocreated with EA and Stakeholder Organization Advisory Boards to ensure relevance, accessibility, and appropriateness. We report on 3 formative surveys, a pilot intervention, protocol development, and the community-engaged process for intervention development. Descriptive statistics were applied to the surveys and pilot intervention baseline results to produce means and SDs using R. Results: We developed posts (n=400) for a Facebook feed aimed at reducing 6 cancer risk behaviors (unhealthy diet, lack of physical activity, tobacco use, alcohol use, sun exposure, and human papillomavirus infection) with iterative input from the EA and stakeholder advisory boards. Formative surveys with rural EAs (n=297) and a pilot study of the intervention with this population (n=26) were conducted. In the pilot study, the intervention reached participants across rural counties, with sustained engagement (post views=1060, reactions=346, comments=72) over a one-month period. Conclusions: This web-based cancer prevention intervention is scalable and delivers engaging, evidence-informed health information to rural EAs. We offer key insights into the design and implementation of web-based cancer prevention interventions for EAs by describing the resources, timelines, and expertise needed to design and implement the intervention. Considerations for fully engaging EA and community stakeholder partners are presented, and we discuss how their involvement resulted in modifications that strengthened the intervention. Finally, we highlight the importance of theory-based health-behavior messaging, digital messaging skillsets, and platform-tailored dissemination strategies for maximizing web-based intervention acceptability. JSON: Name: peak_wellness_pipeline Title: Iterative community-engaged development and pilot evaluation of a theory-based Facebook private-group intervention to reduce six cancer risk behaviors among rural emerging adults Short Hypothesis: Participation in the four-week PEAK Wellness Chat Facebook private-group intervention causes a greater reduction in a predefined composite cancer-risk behavior score (physical inactivity, poor diet, nicotine/tobacco use, risky alcohol use, unprotected UV exposure, and incomplete HPV vaccination) among rural emerging adults aged 18–26 compared with no-intervention control. Related Work: Prior work includes web-based and social-media health behavior interventions, community-based participatory development of public health programs, and media-literacy efforts to counter online misinformation. Social-media interventions have demonstrated feasibility for engagement but show variable effects on sustained behavior change. Existing approaches often lack one or more of the following: explicit behavior-change theory integration, iterative co-creation with target-population advisory boards, platform-tailored content design, transparency of source material, rigorous pilot-to-trial transition documentation, and standardized moderator/engagement protocols. Many prior studies focus on urban or older adult samples, rely on single-format content (eg, text or video only), use cross-sectional evaluation or short pilots without cluster-randomized designs, and report limited operational details (timelines, staffing, post libraries) that impede reproducibility. These gaps limit generalizability to rural emerging adults and reduce comparability across interventions. Abstract: Rural emerging adults (ages 18–26) exhibit multiple modifiable cancer risk behaviors yet are incompletely reached by evidence-based prevention messaging. We propose a structured pipeline for the development, pilot testing, and rigorous evaluation of PEAK Wellness Chat: a theory-driven, community-engaged social media intervention delivered via Facebook private groups. The pipeline integrates behavior-change theory, emergent media-literacy content, and iterative co-creation with emerging-adult and stakeholder advisory boards to produce a dynamic library of platform-tailored posts and moderator protocols. Primary contributions are (1) a reproducible workflow documenting stakeholder engagement, post production, and scheduling; (2) measurable engagement and behavioral outcome metrics for pilot-to-trial progression; and (3) pre-specified experimental contrasts (full intervention versus control and content-feature ablations). Expected outcomes include demonstrable feasibility and engagement in a rural EA population, measurable short-term reductions in a composite cancer-risk behavior score, and a validated protocol suitable for multi-cluster pragmatic evaluation and replication. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Formative dataset: N≈300 rural emerging adults (age 18–26) survey pool for post pretesting and source credibility assessment; (B) Pilot dataset: N≈26 intervention participants for protocol refinement; (C) Main trial dataset: stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial with 20 clusters (rural counties), target N=25 participants per cluster (total N=500), enrolled baseline and followed at 1, 3, and 6 months. Inclusion: RUCC 4–9 counties, active Facebook account, age 18–26. Baselines: (1) No-intervention waitlist control; (2) Attention-control arm receiving generic health information posts (non-tailored); (3) Active comparators in ablation arms (see below). Primary outcome: composite cancer-risk behavior score computed from validated instruments normalized to z-scores (GPAQ for physical activity; dietary screener for fruit/veg and energy from fat; 30-day tobacco/vaping use; AUDIT-C for alcohol misuse; self-reported sunburns/personal protection; HPV vaccine initiation/completion status). Secondary outcomes: engagement metrics (post views, reactions, comments, link clicks, retention), mediators (self-efficacy, perceived source credibility, media-literacy score). Evaluation metrics: mean change in composite score (ANCOVA / linear mixed-effects models), proportion achieving clinically meaningful change (logistic mixed models), time-to-HPV-initiation (Cox model), engagement rates (Poisson/negative binomial models). Experimental setup: stepped-wedge randomization schedule with clusters crossing from control to intervention in randomized steps; participant-level repeated measures; models include random intercepts for clusters and participants, fixed effects for time and covariates. Statistical power: with N=500, ICC=0.02, two-sided alpha=0.05, 80% power to detect standardized mean difference ≈0.25 in composite score. Ablation/comparisons: (A) content-source transparency: posts with explicit evidence links and source labels versus posts without visible sources; (B) format ablation: video microcontent versus static image versus text-only; (C) engagement frequency ablation: 2 posts/day versus 1 post/day; (D) moderator responsiveness ablation: active moderator replies within 24h versus minimal moderation. Analysis plan: pre-registered primary comparison = mean pre-post change during exposure periods vs control periods using mixed-effects modeling; secondary analyses test ablation contrasts and dose–response of engagement metrics; sensitivity analyses for missing data (multiple imputation) and self-report bias (auxiliary validation subsets where feasible). Risk Factors and Limitations: Platform dependence: results limited to Facebook private-group users; algorithm or policy changes may alter reach or data access. Measurement bias: primary behavioral outcomes rely on self-report instruments subject to social desirability and recall error; limited objective validation possible. Selection bias: recruitment via web panels and social media may not represent all rural emerging adults (digital divide, differential platform use). Contamination: informal sharing of posts outside groups may create cross-arm exposure. Scalability constraints: high moderator labor for active engagement and real-time response may limit scaling. Small effect sizes: short-term interventions may produce modest behavior change requiring large sample sizes for detection. Generalizability: findings from Mountain West or RUCC 4–9 sampled counties may not extrapolate to other rural regions or international contexts. Data privacy/regulatory risk: platform data access and participant confidentiality risks, including potential deplatforming or data loss. Emergent misinformation and adversarial manipulation: public comments or coordinated actors could undermine message credibility. Resource variability: iterative co-creation requires sustained time and expert personnel, which may not be reproducible in lower-resource settings.
